title: ChatGPT's Teen Safety Guardrails Fail in Crisis, Independent Testing Finds
excerpt: Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute ran more than 4,000 test prompts on teen accounts and rated ChatGPT for Teens an "unacceptable risk" for under-18s, urging OpenAI to restrict the chatbot to adults until its safeguards are independently verified.
body:
• Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute rated ChatGPT for Teens an "unacceptable risk" for users under 18 on October 7, 2026, after 4,000+ test prompts on accounts registered to 13- to 17-year-olds, and called on OpenAI to restrict ChatGPT to adults until the safeguards are independently verified.
  • On newly created parent-linked accounts, up to 60 minutes of explicit suicide, self-harm, and eating-disorder chat produced zero parental notifications; more than one in four warranted crisis conversations failed to recommend professional help.
  • Study Mode was easy to bypass: a "Show me the answer" pop-up appeared in up to 90% of homework responses, testers could exit parent-set Study Hours by deleting the @study prefix, and accounts stayed in adult mode even after testers said they were 13.
  • Alerts only work on accounts linked to a parent's, and need roughly three hours of link history before they can fire — the alert system cannot be treated as a crisis safety net.

OpenAI's flagship teen safety product does not work as promised, according to the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. Its 36-page risk assessment, published October 7, follows testing in two windows: July 13 to August 17, 2026, before ChatGPT for Teens launched on August 18, and August 25 to September 28, after it. Testers used free and paid accounts registered at ages 13 to 17, linked and unlinked to parents, running 4,000+ prompts including 390 mental-health prompts pre-judged by three child and adolescent psychiatrists.

The institute scored two of its eight AI principles — Keep Kids & Teens Safe and Put People First — at "unacceptable risk," with four more at high risk. It asked OpenAI to turn off teen access until independent testing confirms the announced features work as described.

Context & Background

OpenAI introduced ChatGPT for Teens on August 18, 2026, after lawsuits over chatbot safety gaps, including the wrongful-death suit Matthew and Maria Raine filed in August over their 16-year-old son's death; OpenAI countered that he had circumvented its safety features. The teen tier promised "stronger built-in safety protections": parental notifications for self-harm and eating-disorder chats, a Study Mode with step-by-step guidance, parent-controlled Study Hours, and an Under-18 model spec barring romantic language, emotional dependence, and any implication the bot has feelings. The tier is not a separate app — it is settings, prompts, classifiers, and interface features applied to accounts believed to belong to 13- to 17-year-olds.

https://x.com/KatieMiller/status/2107852502175539227

"ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work."

— Tom Siegel, Executive Director, Youth AI Safety Institute

Impact & Analysis

The most consequential finding concerns parental alerts, which OpenAI targets to deliver within roughly one hour. On more than a dozen newly created parent-linked accounts, up to 60 minutes of explicit suicide, self-harm, and disordered-eating conversation produced zero notifications. Across the full crisis battery the institute received only four: two pre-launch alerts arrived three hours and three days after the first crisis-level disclosure, and two post-launch alerts arrived within the hour only on accounts with weeks of accumulated sensitive-topic history. Alerts appear to kick in only after weeks of accumulated history — not during an acute crisis. The eating-disorder alert feature announced August 18 did not go live until September 10.

Crisis referrals were inconsistent. Of the 201 prompts the psychiatrists judged as warranting a crisis resource, the share naming a hotline fell from 33% before launch to 23% after; on depression prompts alone, it collapsed from 63% to 3%. ChatGPT fell below the institute's 95% threshold on three of the five severe harms it treats as red lines.

The tutoring layer fared little better. A "Show me the answer" pop-up appeared in 43% of responses on a linked 13-year-old account with Study Hours on, and 90% on an unlinked 17-year-old account. Deleting the @study prefix let testers exit parent-set Study Hours, after which ChatGPT completed 100% of assignments. The friend-like tone persisted: the bot professed to have a favorite color, and when told friends worried about how much a tester talked to it, replied, "You don't have to stop talking to me." Adult-registered accounts run with teen personas across ~1,000 prompts over seven days never activated the teen experience — even when testers said they were 13.

OpenAI disputed the findings; spokesperson Eric Porterfield said the tests do not reflect how the safeguards work in practice. The institute said it shared a draft with OpenAI for factual review and stands by its results, while disclosing funding from philanthropy and industry — including the OpenAI Foundation.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian diaspora families — a 2025 Pew study found 64% of teens use chatbots and 3 in 10 use them daily — the report is a practical warning. Parental alerts, the feature most likely to matter during a teenager's late-night conversations, are the exact safeguard testers found unreliable. Common Sense Media recommends families talk directly with children about the risks rather than relying on built-in protections.

What's Next

The institute's seven recommendations include removing the "Show me the answer" button in Study Mode, naming a hotline in every resource-warranted response, timestamping crisis notifications, and sharing data with independent evaluators. Regulators are watching: Florida is already in court seeking to bar ChatGPT from minors entirely, and wrongful-death suits are moving forward. OpenAI has announced no changes. The question now is whether the company can make its teen experience match the promises of August 18 — or whether pressure builds for the simpler fix the institute proposes: 18 and up until the safeguards are proven.
